The Jotnian igneous episode of central-east Sweden is represented by dolerite sills distributed over an area of 5000 km2. The results are combined with other data from the same region to derive an overall mean palaeo- magnetic pole for the Jotnian igneous episode. The optimum demagnetizing temperature vaned between 250 and 300°C at which more than 60 per cent of the natural intensity was retained. The blocking temperatures covered the range from 400 to 600°C. Sediments were also submitted to chemical leaching in which the specimens were immersed in hydrochloric acid (8N) for a given time (8, 31, 107, 270, 470, 700, 990 and 1300 hr), washed in water, measured and then reimmersed in acid (Roy & Park 1974). The leaching rate was optimized by cutting two incisions in each specimen. The optimum demagnetizing chemical leaching time was 700 hr, at which more than 50 per cent of the natural intensity was retained. No substantial differences between the directions of the stable remanence isolated during the thermal and chemical cleaning were observed, (Fig. 2). The stable remanence of the basaltic lava flow and the underlying baked sedimentary rocks were isolated by detailed alternating field demagnetization. The optimum de- magnetizing AC field was 200 Oe at which more than 80 per cent of the NRM intensity was retained. Three samples from the Amana-Talampaya Formation showed anisotropic RM; it was not possible to isolate stable remanence in these samples. No substantial differences between the directions of the stable remanence isolated during the thermal and chemical cleaning were observed, (Fig. 2). The stable remanence of the basaltic lava flow and the underlying baked sedimentary rocks were isolated by detailed alternating field demagnetization. The optimum de- magnetizing AC field was 200 Oe at which more than 80 per cent of the NRM intensity was retained. Three samples from the Amana-Talampaya Formation showed anisotropic RM; it was not possible to isolate stable remanence in these samples. in the Kavirondian and the Nyanzian Systems of the Western Province. The Nyanzian and the Kavirondian Systems are presumed to be the oldest Precambrian rocks in Kenya. The Kavirondian System unconformably overlies the Nyanzian System. The rocks of both the systems were folded after the deposition of the Kavirondian System (Cahen & Snelling 1966). These two systems have suffered thermal metamorphism due to the intrusions of the granites. In general, the texture of the granites varies from fine to extremely coarse grained. The usual colour of the granites is mottled pink or white and black. The pink colour has been attributed either to hematite flakes in feldspar or to an iron-rich solution derived elsewhere (Pulfrey 1945). The coarse-grain variety carries closely packed large ‘salmon’ type feldspar phenocrysts. Quartz is generally interstitial and often occurs as granular aggregates with the feldspar. The dark minerals are usually hornblende and biotite. The accessories are apatite and sphene. Pulfrey (1 945) suggested the possibility that there is more than one intrusion in the Mumias granite, west of Broderick Falls (Fig. 1). The polished section petrology showed that the specimens of all the sites contained titanomagnetite grains of size ranging from about 50-350 pm in diameter. In a few cases the grain boundaries were corroded and possessed inclusions of silicate minerals. High- temperature oxidation of the grains, class 2 type of Ade Hall er al.'s (1968) classification, was observed only in specimens of sites 5 and 11. Ilmenite lamellae were exsolved in the titanomagnetite grains. Highly corroded titanomagnetite grains in the specimens of sites 8 and 12 were partly replaced by a hematite phase. The average Curie temperatures of the specimens of these two sites were obtained at 600 and 59OoC, respectively, which confirmed the presence of hematite. The

During the last few years more palaeomagnetic results of the Precambrian rocks from other parts of Africa have been published. Piper et ~l. (1973) defined a single apparent polar wander swathe for the interval 2300- 1950 Ma using the palaeomagnetic results from the Kaapvaal, Congo and West African cratons. They suggested that the principal cratonic areas of Africa have been approximately in the present relative positions and orientations since 2200 Ma. The results show that the formation has mixed polarity. The k/ksig. ratio for site 3 remained below unity at all fields of demagnetization. It was observed that the mean sample directions of this site remained scattered with individual specimens moving erratically in an unstable fashion. Consequently, this site was considered random and discarded from the final analysis. All the other sites are significant on the basis of the criterion used. Site 6 gave a good 'reversed' direction and its polarity was reversed in the evaluation of the mean direction of the significant sites. Sites 8 and 12 apparently gave stable directions but their divergences from the group mean direction are extremely large. Therefore it is unlikely that they belong to the population sampled. Besides this, the natural reinanence of the specimens from these two sites is suspected to be of a secondary origin (refer to Section 4.2). The thin sections showed a preponderance of a hematitic alteration product, a scarcity of original magnetite, as well as a very fine-grained (< 1 pm in diameter), optically unidentifiable, opaque phase. The low initial intensities observed in the demagnetization studies are in agreement with the predominance of hematite. However, the low-temperature and characteristic components were removed below or by the Curie temperature of magnetite (c. 580°C). Thus, the hematite may be the result of two different alterations and be rich in titanium. The latter is also suggested optically by occasional inter- growths of hematite and rutile. The high-temperature component seen in Fig. 7 was removed near the magnetite Curie point. In other samples it was removed near or above 580°C. Thus, the carrier of this high-temperature component must be relatively pure iron oxide and may be associated with the unidentified fine-grained opaque phase, perhaps ‘primary’ in origin. The Armorican Massif was selected for sampling due to prevalence of relatively un- metamorphozed Palaeozoic sediments preserved in the synclines of Normandy and Brittany. The Massif is divided into a series of domains separated by fault systems trending E-W to ESE-WNW (Fig. 2, inset). The two northernmost domains, the Domnonean domain and the Mancellian domain, are thought to have been virtually unaffected or only moderately affected respectively by the Hercynian deformation and metamorphism (CognB 1974), and thus they appeared to be well suited for palaeomagnetic investigation. Devonian redbeds were sampled from the Syncline of Montmartin (Group A) in Normandy, Cambro- Ordovician redbeds and trachyandesites were sampled in the areas of PaimpolLBrBhec (Group B) and Erquy-Cap Frkhel (Group C) in northern Brittany. Samples of Late Cambrian to Early Ordovician redbeds were taken from the Syncline of the Zone Bocaine (Group D) in Normandy. All three Cambro-Ordovician units studied yielded characteristic directions of magnetization that are interpreted as remagnetizations of Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous age on the basis of negative fold tests, similarities with the directions of the Late Devonian redbeds, reset K/Ar ages of 345 MA, or the occurrence of significant high- temperature magnetizations. A significant separation between the Armorican Massif and Gondwanaland, on the other hand, suggests that an intervening middle Palaeozoic ocean existed which subsequently was consumed by subduction somewhere to the south of the Armorican Massif. r such a comparison through most of the later Palaeozoic. The present study was undertaken to obtain palaeo- magnetic data for Hercynian Europe to complete the comparison. The Armorican Massif was selected for sampling due to prevalence of relatively un- metamorphozed Palaeozoic sediments preserved in the synclines of Normandy and Brittany. The Massif is divided into a series of domains separated by fault systems trending E-W to ESE-WNW (Fig. 2, inset). The two northernmost domains, the Domnonean domain and the Mancellian domain, are thought to have been virtually unaffected or only moderately affected respectively by the Hercynian deformation and metamorphism (CognB 1974), and thus they appeared to be well suited for palaeomagnetic investigation. Devonian redbeds were sampled from the Syncline of Montmartin (Group A) in Normandy, Cambro- Ordovician redbeds and trachyandesites were sampled in the areas of PaimpolLBrBhec (Group B) and Erquy-Cap Frkhel (Group C) in northern Brittany. Samples of Late Cambrian to Early Ordovician redbeds were taken from the Syncline of the Zone Bocaine (Group D) in Normandy. In order to test plate tectonic hypotheses for the Hercynian orogeny in western Europe, Late Devonian and Cambro-Ordovician redbeds and volcanics have been palaeomagnetically studied. The Late Devonian redbeds show nearly univectorial remanent magnetizations during stepwise thermal, chemical and alternating field demagnetization and yield a pole position at 19.8' N, 144.2' E. All three Cambro-Ordovician units studied yielded characteristic directions of magnetization that are inter

erately affected respectively by the Hercynian deformation and metamorphism (CognB 1974), and thus they appeared to be well suited for palaeomagnetic investigation. Devonian redbeds were sampled from the Syncline of Montmartin (Group A) in Normandy, Cambro- Ordovician redbeds and trachyandesites were sampled in the areas of PaimpolLBrBhec (Group B) and Erquy-Cap Frkhel (Group C) in northern Brittany. Samples of Late Cambrian to Early Ordovician redbeds were taken from the Syncline of the Zone Bocaine (Group D) in Normandy. The geology and relative ages of the individual areas will be discussed with the results. Sampling and laboratory techniques All sites but one were drilled in the field and oriented with

In addition to demagnetization studies, polished thin sections of seven trachyandesite samples were examined. The thin sections showed a preponderance of a hematitic alteration product, a scarcity of original magnetite, as well as a very fine-grained (< 1 pm in diameter), optically unidentifiable, opaque phase. 288 Introduction Interpretation of past orogenies in a plate tectonic context is valuable in expanding knowledge of plate tectonic theory and of specific orogenic processes. Some orogenies readily lend themselves to a tectonic subduction and/or collision interpretation. Others, such as the Late Palaeozoic Hercynian orogeny of western Europe, are enigmatic. The Hercynian orogenic belt lacks many of the typical tectonic indicators of subduction and collision and has characteristics not easily explained in plate tectonic terms. The Hercynian belt has few or no high-pressure, low-temperature metamorphic indicators, ophiolites or ultrabasites. Nappe structures are rare. Metamorphism is shallow. In addition, the orogenic belt is very wide (approximately 1000 km) and contains abundant granites and migmatites (Zwart 1967). The difficulty in placing the Hercynian orogeny into a plate tectonic model can be seen in the number of locations of proposed subduction zones (Fig. 1) and the suggested styles and timing of closure. a plate tectonic model can be seen in the number of locations of proposed subduction zones (Fig. 1) and the suggested styles and timing of closure. The plate tectonic models can be divided into three groups: (1) those proposing the closure of an ocean to the north of the Armorican Massif separating stable or northern Europe from Hercynian or central and southern Europe ending in a continent-continent collision (Johnson 1973, 1974; Dewey & Burke 1973; Burrett 1972; in part, McKerrow & Ziegler 1972; in part, Burne 1973), (2) those proposing the closure of an ocean to the south of Hercynian Europe in an Andean-type subduction, later the site of the Alpine orogeny (Nicolas 1972; Floyd 1972), and (3) those proposing the existence of more than one ocean where Hercynian Europe or parts of it acted as microplates between or attached to stable Europe and the Gondwana continents (Laurent 1972; Riding 1974; Badham & Halls 1975; in part, Floyd 1972). In general, proponents of subduction maintain that closure of an intervening ocean or oceans was occurring during the Late Devonian and/or Early Carboniferous with final collision in the early Late Carboniferous. Those high-temperature directions from the Cambro- Ordovician redbeds and volcanics that are relatively well grouped are interpreted as original Cambro-Ordov

r such a comparison through most of the later Palaeozoic. The present study was undertaken to obtain palaeo- magnetic data for Hercynian Europe to complete the comparison. The Armorican Massif was selected for sampling due to prevalence of relatively un- metamorphozed Palaeozoic sediments preserved in the synclines of Normandy and Brittany. The Massif is divided into a series of domains separated by fault systems trending E-W to ESE-WNW (Fig. 2, inset). The two northernmost domains, the Domnonean domain and the Mancellian domain, are thought to have been virtually unaffected or only moderately affected respectively by the Hercynian deformation and metamorphism (CognB 1974), and thus they appeared to be well suited for palaeomagnetic investigation. Devonian redbeds were sampled from the Syncline of Montmartin (Group A) in Normandy, Cambro- Ordovician redbeds and trachyandesites were sampled in the areas of PaimpolLBrBhec (Group B) and Erquy-Cap Frkhel (Group C) in northern Brittany. Douglas Peninsula Formation The Douglas Peninsula Formation, the lowest formation of the Pethei Group, occurs throughout the aulacogen and varies in thickness from 16-33 m (Hoffman 1968). Douglas Peninsula Formation The Douglas Peninsula Formation, the lowest formation of the Pethei Group, occurs throughout the aulacogen and varies in thickness from 16-33 m (Hoffman 1968). The type section was sampled. It is 25 m thick and it is autochthonous (Hoffman er al. 1977). The rock is a thin-bedded, fissile, red marlstone, that is composed of small lenticles of pink or brown limestone in dark reddish-brown mudstone. The dominant opaque mineral is haematite, which occurs as a dusting on sedimentary grains, and as very fine blebs on sand grain boundaries. There are detrital grains of haematite, up to 50 pm in diameter. Haematite, leucoxene and rare remnants of ilmenite, occur in the matrix as blocky grains that range in diameter from 10-50 pm. The supracrustal rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline and associated aulacogen contain upwards of 10 000 m of rocks with good strati- graphic control. In this paper new palaeomagnetic poles from four rock units are described, bringing the total from the sequence to 10. The poles are as follows: Seton Formation 02" N, 093' W, Ag3 = 6', Rb/Sr isochron - 1870 Ma; Douglas Peninsula Formation 17" S, 102" W, Ag5 = 16"; Takiyuak Forma- tion 13" S, l l low, Ag5 = 8"; Peninsular sill 22" S, 097" W, Ag5 = 7", Rb/Sr isochron - 1800 Ma. Overprinted magnetizations from the Seton and Douglas Peninsula Formations are described. The poles from the Coronation Geo- syncline delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and it is argued that there is no basis in the palaeomagnetic evidence for the proposition that the continental crust was assembled into a single unchanged pangaea during the whole of the interval - 2200 to ~ 1300 Ma. . Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. The supracrustal rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline and associated aulacogen contain upwards of 10 000 m of rocks with good strati- graphic control. In this paper new palaeomagnetic poles from four rock units are described, bringing the total from the sequence to 10. The poles are as follows: Seton Formation 02" N, 093' W, Ag3 = 6', Rb/Sr isochron - 1870 Ma; Douglas Peninsula Formation 17" S, 102" W, Ag5 = 16"; Takiyuak Forma- tion 13" S, l l low, Ag5 = 8"; Peninsular sill 22" S, 097" W, Ag5 = 7", Rb/Sr isochron - 1800 Ma. Overprinted magnetizations from the Seton and Douglas Peninsula Formations are described. The poles from the Coronation Geo- syncline delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and

line delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and it is argued that there is no basis in the palaeomagnetic evidence for the proposition that the continental crust was assembled into a single unchanged pangaea during the whole of the interval - 2200 to ~ 1300 Ma. . Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. McGlynn Earth Physics Branch and fhe Geological Survey of Canada, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa, Canada Received 1978 December 4;in original form 1976 September 6 Summary. The supracrustal rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline and associated aulacogen contain upwards of 10 000 m of rocks with good strati- graphic control. In this paper new palaeomagnetic poles from four rock units are described, bringing the total from the sequence to 10. The poles are as follows: Seton Formation 02" N, 093' W, Ag3 = 6', Rb/Sr isochron - 1870 Ma; Douglas Peninsula Formation 17" S, 102" W, Ag5 = 16"; Takiyuak Forma- tion 13" S, l l low, Ag5 = 8"; Peninsular sill 22" S, 097" W, Ag5 = 7", Rb/Sr isochron - 1800 Ma. Overprinted magnetizations from the Seton and Douglas Peninsula Formations are described. The poles from the Coronation Geo- syncline delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and

line delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and it is argued that there is no basis in the palaeomagnetic evidence for the proposition that the continental crust was assembled into a single unchanged pangaea during the whole of the interval - 2200 to ~ 1300 Ma. . Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. We have therefore sampled only from those regions that geological mapping indicates are autochthonous. The Coronation G

The supracrustal rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline and associated aulacogen contain upwards of 10 000 m of rocks with good strati- graphic control. In this paper new palaeomagnetic poles from four rock units are described, bringing the total from the sequence to 10. The poles are as follows: Seton Formation 02" N, 093' W, Ag3 = 6', Rb/Sr isochron - 1870 Ma; Douglas Peninsula Formation 17" S, 102" W, Ag5 = 16"; Takiyuak Forma- tion 13" S, l l low, Ag5 = 8"; Peninsular sill 22" S, 097" W, Ag5 = 7", Rb/Sr isochron - 1800 Ma. Overprinted magnetizations from the Seton and Douglas Peninsula Formations are described. The poles from the Coronation Geo- syncline delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and

line delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and it is argued that there is no basis in the palaeomagnetic evidence for the proposition that the continental crust was assembled into a single unchanged pangaea during the whole of the interval - 2200 to ~ 1300 Ma. . Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. We have therefore sampled only from those regions that geological mapping indicates are autochthonous. The Coronation G

th, H Hepburn Metamorphic and Plutonic Complex, E Epworth Group in the Epworth basin, K Kilohigok Basin, and the Athapuscow Aulacogen that contains the Great Slave Supergroup (GSS). Ages of rocks are as follows: (1) Archaean of the Slave Structural Province, (2) Aphebian of the Coronation Geosyncline, (3) Helikian and Hadrynian cover rocks, (4) Phanerozoic rocks. The Stark Formation is generally brecciated. 326 Bingham & Evans (1976) have suggested that one possible explanation of the westerly positions of the Stark and Tochatwi poles is that they have been rotated clockwise about a local vertical axis. They note that the bedding strikes at the Stark and Tochatwi localities in block Z differ systematically from those in adjacent parts of the aulacogen, and they calculate that an anticlockwise tectonic rotation of 60" would bring the strikes into agree- ment. This rotation would place the Stark and Tochatwi poles at about 18" S, 83OW. Their prediction is in excellent agreement with results reported here. The predicted position is midway between poles we have found for the Takiyuak (TK) and Pearson (PA) Formations (Fig. 11). The Takiyuak Formation is the correlative of the Tochatwi in the Coronation Geosyncline and is autochthonous (Hoffman 1973). The Pearson Formation is the near time equivalent of the Tochatwi. The Pearson Formation has been sampled palaeomagnetically from an autochthonous region about 8 km north of block Z (McClynn & Irving 1978). We believe this to be good evidence in favour of the rotation hypothesis as originally suggested on structural grounds by Bingham & Evans (1976). Recently

ction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. The Coronation Geosyncline (Hoffman 1973) developed in later Aphebian time (approxi- mately -~ 2000 to - 1700 Ma) along the north-west border of Laurentia. The supracrustal rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline and associated aulacogen contain upwards of 10 000 m of rocks with good strati- graphic control. In this paper new palaeomagnetic poles from four rock units are described, bringing the total from the sequence to 10. The poles are as follows: Seton Formation 02" N, 093' W, Ag3 = 6', Rb/Sr isochron - 1870 Ma; Douglas Peninsula Formation 17" S, 102" W, Ag5 = 16"; Takiyuak Forma- tion 13" S, l l low, Ag5 = 8"; Peninsular sill 22" S, 097" W, Ag5 = 7", Rb/Sr isochron - 1800 Ma. Overprinted magnetizations from the Seton and Douglas Peninsula Formations are described. The poles from the Coronation Geo- syncline delineate a polar loop - the Coronation loop. Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and

Two previously observed poles from the Stark and Tochatwi do not fall on this loop and new evidence is presented which indicates that they have been affected by local rotations. Comparisons are made with results from Africa and Australia, and it is argued that there is no basis in the palaeomagnetic evidence for the proposition that the continental crust was assembled into a single unchanged pangaea during the whole of the interval - 2200 to ~ 1300 Ma. . Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. We present new palaeomagnetic results from the Coronation Geosyncline, and use these, along with previously published results, to construct a path of apparent polar wander (APW) relative to Laurentia. We then compare this path with those obtained by other workers for other continents in order to evaluate the concept of a Proterozoic super- continent. One major problem is that of the relative rotation of small blocks. Palaeomagnetic results from such blocks yield aberrant pole positions that cannot be used to construct paths of apparent polar wandering. We have therefore sampled only from those regions that geological mapping indicates are autochthonous. The Coronation G

Douglas Peninsula Formation The Douglas Peninsula Formation, the lowest formation of the Pethei Group, occurs throughout the aulacogen and varies in thickness from 16-33 m (Hoffman 1968). The type section was sampled. It is 25 m thick and it is autochthonous (Hoffman er al. 1977). The rock is a thin-bedded, fissile, red marlstone, that is composed of small lenticles of pink or brown limestone in dark reddish-brown mudstone. The dominant opaque mineral is haematite, which occurs as a dusting on sedimentary grains, and as very fine blebs on sand grain boundaries. autochthonous zone. The Takiyuak Formation occurs only in the autochthonous zone, and is the youngest unit of the Epworth Group (Table 1). It is the molasse phase of the geosyncline, and comprises immature terrigenous sediments deposited in an alluvial environ- ment (Hoffman 1973). The total thickness is about 600 m, and in the sampling area the beds have a regional dip of 10" to the south-west. The basal units consist of red mudstones and siltstones, which grade upward into mudstones and thickly bedded lithic sandstones. Lithic clasts include clastic and carbonate sediments, silicic volcanic rocks and plutonic and metamorphic rocks. Haematite is the most abundant oxide, occurring as dust on silicate sedimentary grains, as fine blades (5 pm or less) distributed around sedimentary grains, and as rounded detrital grains up to 300pm in diameter composed of crystalline specular haematite or amorphous or earthy haematite. Haematite also occurs in the lithic fragments, in which the grains have lamellae of haematite and leucoxene with octahedral texture, which probably results from the alteration of grains of magnetite with ilmenite lamellae, during sedimentation. Most of the samples (65 per cent) studied by Cough et al. (1977) in the Snowdrift area are from two sections. The Tochatwi section (45 specimens) from Tochatwi Island have K1 directions similar to those in the Kahochella rocks of Keith Island, and the fabric is considered to be depositional from their 4 and f values. As noted above this Tochatwi section is not located in block Z and the remanence directions are not depositional but are secondary (Evans & Bingham 1976). The second section is from the Stark Formation (47 specimens) of block Z. It has remanence directions that are regarded as primary (Bingham & Evans 1976), and the K1 axes are about 60" different from those in the Kahochella. However, K1 is close to the fold axis and 4 and fare such that Cough et al. (1977) argue that the fabric is secondary. It would appear therefore that the results from these two well- sampled sections provide no information regarding the cause of the westerly displace poles of block Z, because in the one (Tochatwi) the remanence is apparently secondary, and in the other (Stark) the susceptibility fabric is apparently secondary. Introduction In this paper we are concerned with mid-Proterozoic events in the interval about - 2 100 to - 1700 Ma. The John O'Groats Sandstone, on the north-east tip of Scotland, is the uppermost unit of a thick Old Red Sandstone sequence from the uppermost Middle Devonian. Samples from 13 sites have been treated by thermal and acid leaching techniques making use of the convergence of re- magnetization circles when stable end points were not reached. In some cases, in which the magnetic constituents were asymmetrically distributed, splitting the specimens proved useful. Two axes of magnetization have been identified. The easiest to determine, called the A axis, is present most frequently in the reversed sense, at roughly Dec 190°, Inc - 40". The normal component can also be detected as stable end points on acid leaching. The A-axis magnetization is carried mainly by the pigmented cement. The B axis, which is aligned NNE-SSW and almost horizontal, is less well defined. Both the A- and B-axis orientations cited are after making corrections for structural tilts that are present at some of the sites. The direction of the B-axis magnetization agrees well with that of other Devonian units from west of the Great Glen Fault and is interpreted as having been acquired during, or shortly after, deposition. The A magnetization is interpreted as having been acquired during the Mesozoic, probably associated with regional burial and subsequent tectonic uplift of the area during the Jurassic. The John O'Groats Sandstone, on the north-east tip of Scotland, is the uppermost unit of a thick Old Red Sandstone sequence from the uppermost Middle Devonian. Samples from 13 sites have been treated by thermal and acid leaching techniques making use of the convergence of re- magnetization circles when stable end points were not reached. In some cases, in which the magnetic constituents were asymmetrically distributed, splitting the specimens proved useful. Two axes of magnetization have been identified. The easiest to determine, called the A axis, is present most frequently in the reversed sense, at roughly Dec 190°, Inc - 40". The normal component can also be detected as stable end points on acid leaching. The A-axis magnetization is carried mainly by the pigmented cement. The B axis, which is aligned NNE-SSW and almost horizontal, is less well defined. Both the A- and B-axis orientations cited are after making corrections for structural tilts that are present at some of the sites. The direction of the B-axis magnetization agrees well with that of other Devonian units from west of the Great Glen Fault and is interpreted as having been acquired during, or shortly after, deposition. The A magnetization is interpreted as having been acquired during the Mesozoic, probably associated with regional burial and subsequent tectonic uplift of the area during the Jurassic. al record of Precambrian metamorphism, uplift and cooling. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of such a terrain comprising the central part of the Lewisian foreland of NW Scotland. In Proterozoic times this formed a peripheral part of the much larger Laurentian Shield, a cratonic region comprising the Precambrian basement of North America and Greenland (Bridgwater, Watson & Windley 1973). 2 Geology 2.1 REGIONAL SETTING The Precambrian Lewisian basement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/ granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath, Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode (Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other compositions. sement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/ granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath, Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode (Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other compositions. The dykes were first used by Sutton &Watson (1951) to separate a pre-dyke (Scourian) mobile episode from a post-dyke (Laxfordian) mobile episode. They are now wholly or partly amphibolitized, and are foliated to variable degrees in those parts of the Lewisian affected by the Laxfordian episode, although some relict igneous textures are usually present. al record of Precambrian metamorphism, uplift and cooling. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of such a terrain comprising the central part of the Lewisian foreland of NW Scotland. In Proterozoic times this formed a peripheral part of the much larger Laurentian Shield, a cratonic region comprising the Precambrian basement of North America and Greenland (Bridgwater, Watson & Windley 1973). 2 Geology 2.1 REGIONAL SETTING The Precambrian Lewisian basement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/ granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath, Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode (Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other compositions. al record of Precambrian metamorphism, uplift and cooling. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of such a terrain comprising the central part of the Lewisian foreland of NW Scotland. In Proterozoic times this formed a peripheral part of the much larger Laurentian Shield, a cratonic region comprising the Precambrian basement of North America and Greenland (Bridgwater, Watson & Windley 1973). 2 Geology 2.1 REGIONAL SETTING The Precambrian Lewisian basement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/ granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath, Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode (Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other compositions. In Proterozoic times this formed a peripheral part of the much larger Laurentian Shield, a cratonic region comprising the Precambrian basement of North America and Greenland (Bridgwater, Watson & Windley 1973). 2 Geology 2.1 REGIONAL SETTING The Precambrian Lewisian basement of NW Scotland, which includes the mainland north of Skye and the Outer Hebrides, forms a foreland zone to the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 550-380 Ma). It comprises quartzo-feldspathic gneisses affected by amphibolite/ granulite metamorphism during an early Scourian episode of crustal incrementation and metamorphism, known as the Badcallian, at approximately 2900--2700 Ma (Moorbath, Welke & Gale 1969); little new material has been added to the complex since this episode (Watson 1975). More restricted reactivation of the Lewisian took place during a late Scourian (Inverian) episode at c. 2300-2200 Ma, and widespread intrusion of NW-SE dykes took place in late- and post-Inverian times; these are predominantly tholeiitic in composition but include a later suite of picrite dykes in addition to a number of other compositions. mplex is emplaced in rocks belonging to the allochthonous Western Complex (e.g. Gee 1975) of the southern Scandinavian Caledonides. The gabbro intrudes metasediments and metavolcanics of the Fundsjd group, which may correlate with the Stq5ren group to the west (eg. Roberts, Springer & Wolff 1970), and the Ordovician (Tremadocian) fossil Dictyonema flabelliforme has been found in rocks of the aureole (Vogt 1940). The gabbro hornfelsed tightly folded rocks and has inclusions of folded country rocks, so the intrusion clearly post-dates at least one fold phase. A contact meta- morphic aureole with index-minerals cordierite, sillimanite and andalusite is developed, with additional garnet present throughout. The peak of regional metamorphism was reached shortly after the emplacement of the complex and was accompanied by the main deforma- tion phase in the area (Olesen et al. 1973). In the western part of the aureole the contact metamorphic assemblages are overprinted by regional assemblages such as andalusite being replaced by kyanite and sillimanite by staurolite and white mica. Titanomagnetite (30 mol per cent ulvospinel) normally dominates over ilmenite (0-2 mol per cent haematite). Two microstructural varieties can be distinguished; ilmenite and titanomagnetite occurring as intercumulus grains interstitial to silicates, and subhedral to euhedral cumulus grains in which titanomagnetite dominates over ilmenite. The grain size of the cumulus Fe-Ti oxides ranges from 1 mm to below 0.05 mm. Two types of titanomagnetite are found, the first indicating an early stage of ulvospinel exsolution and the second a sub-solidus oxidation of ulvospinel at high temperature during magmatic or late-magmatic c

olidus reaction (Krause & Pape 1975). Haematite exsolution is not observed, which according to Ramdohr (1969) indicates less than 6 per cent Fe203 in the ilmenite-haematite solid solution series. Sulphides occur in amounts less than 2 per cent of the total opaque phase in the cumulus magnetite zone. Pyrrhotite is the dominant sulphide and may contribute to the remanence in a few cases. It occurs in interstitial to subhedral aggregates with minor amounts of pent- landite and chalcopyrite with sub-solidus exsolution microstructures. Secondary magnetite, and to a lesser extent ilmenite, is formed during late-magmatic replacement of olivine with magnetite- orthopyroxene symplectites or by reactions between olivine and plagioclase. The magnetite occurs with the silicates in a vermicular to tabular symplectic intergrowth or as irregular grains from a few microns to mm-size often surround- ing partly or completely altered olivine. Magnetite and ilmenite are also found as tabular to acicular grains along the prismatic cleavage in the pyroxenes. Magnetite is only altered to a relatively minor degree with a weak marginal decomposition to goethte in some instances. Comparison of the precisions of in situ and dipcorrected groupings of B3 directions determined from endpoints and vector analysis implies with 95 per cent confidence (Cox 1969) that component B3 was acquired in most sites before Westphalian folding of the redbeds. The dip-corrected mean direction (Fig. 6) of B3 for seven sites (10 specimens) is D = 216", I = 41" (ag5= lo"), which yields a palaeo- magnetic pole at 324"E 11"s (Table 5). One specimen from each site was progressively af demagnetized in peak fields up to 160mT. The NRM of the red shales and grits from Normandy, Jersey and central and southern Brittany generally decayed only slightly during af demagnetization and yielded endpoints close to the direction of total NRM (Fig. 3) as expected where specular hematite or hematite pigment is the dominant magnetic phase. estigations of Mesozoic rocks exposed along the Transantarctic Mountains, The present study adds further palaeo- magnetic information to this period by describing results of palaeomagnetic investigations of Upper Triassic and Middle to Upper Jurassic igneous rocks from Vestfjella, Dronning Maud Land. Vestfjella is situated on an ice-covered peninsula extending into the Weddell Sea and con- stitutes some of the northernmost exposures of the Transantarctic Mountains. It consists of a large number of nunataks, rising up to 400m above the ice-cover, and extending in a NNE-SSW direction for some 130 km. The dominant rock type is subaerial basaltic lava flows, ranging in thickness from 1 to 25 m, dipping slightly to the WNW and building up a sequence of estimated stratigraphic thickness of around 2500 m (Furnes & Mitchell 1978). The lava flows are rather altered, reflected both by a greenish colour and the presence of an assemblage of secondary minerals such as quartz, calcite, prehnite and epidote. Field evidence suggests that this alteration, which apparently becomes more pronounced towards the base of the succession, is due to syn- and/or post-volcanic hydrothermal activity (Furnes & Mitchell 1978). The lava pile is cut by a large number of steeply dipping basaltic dykes 0.

To understand the nature and composition of the remanent magnetization of the dykes the following should be borne in mind, as demonstrated for the RF' dykes: (1) Two main components of magnetization in the RF' dykes have been found -a stable component of high coercivity with a negative inclination and far from the direction of any recent geomagnetic field, and an unstable component in the direction of easiest magnetiza- tion with a positive inclination and close to the present geomagnetic field. The overall picture is more complicated, but in the main the following conclusions seem reasonable : The NRM of the RP dykes consists of a stable primary component and an unstable secondary component. The secondary component has been induced by recent geomagnetic fields and has been deflected into the direction of easiest magnetization. This component is carried by the larger, multi-domain magnetic grains, and so it is of low coercivity. The very hard primary magnetization consequently must be associated with small single-domain or pseudo-single-domain grains of almost pure magnetite, which are too small to be examined in the microprobe. The primary magnetization may also be carried by lamellae of Fe-rich titanomagnetites exsolved in the larger grains. This is supported by the discrepancy demon- strated between calculated and observed T,. A record of geomagnetic field polarity for the Barremian, Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous has been derived in three over- lapping sections of pelagic carbonate rocks in the Umbrian Apennines of northern Italy. The remanence carrier in the greyish-white Majolica limestone and Fucoid Marls is magnetite, with haematite also an important constituent in a zone of ‘couches rouges’ within the Fucoid Marls. The weak remanent magnetizations were measured with a cryogenic magnetometer. Alternating field or thermal demagnetization was used to isolate the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) in 655 specimens from 248 stratigraphic levels. The samples respond positively to a tectonic fold test, indicating that the ChRM predates the Late Tertiary folding of the Umbrian sequence. The magnetic stratigraphy derived from variations of virtual geomagnetic pole latitude clearly defines the recognizable reversal pattern associated with Mesozoic marine magnetic anomalies MO to M4. The sections have been zones palaeon- tologically on the basis of planktonic foraminifera and calcareous nannofossil assemblages. The ages of magnetic anomalies MO to M4 determined in t

ing prohibit development of a magnetic reversal sequence from stratigraphically unrelated samples. On the other hand recent major improvements in magnetometer technology now permit rapid and accurate investigation of sedimentary sequences whose remanent magnetizations were previously measurable only with great difficulty or not at all. Particularly well suited for magnetic stratigraphy studies are sequences of pelagic carbonate rocks. The sequence of geomagnetic reversals derived from the Late Cretaceous anomalies 34 to 29 has been confirmed recently in the Scaglia Rossa pelagic limestone at Gubbio in the Northern Apennines of Italy (Lowrie & Alvarez 1977a,b) and verified in a nearby check section at Moria (Fig. 1) (Alvarez & Lowrie 1978). The reversals were correlated to the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages by palaeontological zonation of the Gubbio section (Premoli Silva 1977) which has been established as a magnetostratigraphic type section for the Late Cretaceous (Alvarez et al. 1977). The Gubbio and Moria sections also confirmed the existence of a long period of normal geomagnetic polarity preceding anomaly 34 which could be correlated with the Cretaceous magnetic quiet zone. According to the oceanic anomaly record the onset of the Cretaceous quiet interval marks

gnetostratigraphic type section for the Late Cretaceous (Alvarez et al. 1977). The Gubbio and Moria sections also confirmed the existence of a long period of normal geomagnetic polarity preceding anomaly 34 which could be correlated with the Cretaceous magnetic quiet zone. According to the oceanic anomaly record the onset of the Cretaceous quiet interval marks the termination of the Mesozoic reversal sequence (Larsor. & Pitman 1972). The youngest anomaly of this sequence is designated MO and has been assigned a Late Aptian age (Larson & Hilde 1975). Recent magnetic stratigraphy studies ir, the Southern (Vicentinian) Alps by Channell, Lowrie & Medizza (1979) have cast doubt on this date. They derived a magnetic stratigraphy in the Early Cretaceous Biancone limestone, in which MO was dated at the base of the Aptian. The present investigation was undertaken to confirm and date the youngest reversals of the Mesozoic sequence, in particular to determine the age of anomaly MO. These new studies have been carried out in three partially overlapping sections of pelagic carbonate rocks at Poggio le Guaine, Valdorbia and Gorgo a Cerbara in the Umbrian Apennines of northern Italy (Fig. 1). Data from a single site in the Valdorbia section were incorporated in a compo- site polar wan

a by VandenBerg, Klootwijk &Wonders (1978). This Late Aptian site was reversely magnetized, but we will show that this Valdorbia reversal does not correspond to anomaly MO. 2 Lithostratigraphy and sampling scheme In the Umbrian sequence the Late Cretaceous is represented by the greyish-white, Ceno- manian to mid-Turonian, Scaglia Rianca limestone and the pink-to-red Scaglia Rossa lime- stone which extends from the mid-Turonian through the remaining Late Cretaceous stages and, indeed, was deposited until the Middle Eocene. The magnetic stratigraphy of these pelagic limestones was developed and checked in the Gubbio and Moria sections (Lowrie & Alvarez 1977a, b; Alvarez 8i Lowrie 1978). The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) is dependent upon the lithology (Fig. 4). Stable natural remanent magnetization (NRM) in the Jersey Volcanics and in a single rhyolite dyke was probably acquired during the Cambrian before folding of the volcanics in the Cadomian Orogeny. After dip correction, the volcanics yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 323" E, 52" N (dp = 33", dm=35"). In Jersey dolerite dykes three groups of stable NRM direc- tions are recognized, with palaeomagnetic poles at 248' E, 26" N (dp = lo", dm = 20°), 339" E, 1" S (dp = 9", dm = 12"),

during the Cambrian before folding of the volcanics in the Cadomian Orogeny. After dip correction, the volcanics yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 323" E, 52" N (dp = 33", dm=35"). In Jersey dolerite dykes three groups of stable NRM direc- tions are recognized, with palaeomagnetic poles at 248' E, 26" N (dp = lo", dm = 20°), 339" E, 1" S (dp = 9", dm = 12"), and 336" E, 31" S (dp = 5", dm = 9"). Comparison with the European apparent polar wander path implies that stable NRM in these groups was acquired respectively during Late Precambrian or early Cambrian, Siluro-Devonian and middle Carboniferous time. The stable NRM of the Jersey lamprophyre dykes yields a palaeomag- netic pole at 322" E, 16" N (dp = 31°, dm = 38") and is probably of Silurian or Devonian age. These palaeomagnetic poles and other new data determined by the author for the Armorican Massif can be fitted to a common apparent polar wander path for Europe, and this implies that the basement of Lower Palaeozoic Europe extended from the Baltic Shield at least as far south as the Armorican Massif. The Hercynian Orogeny in these parts of Europe was therefore probably intracratonic. Table 3 gives the palaeomagnetic parameters such as mean direction of magnetization, VGP positions, palaeolatitude and palaeorotation etc. for all the formations studied so far, for the Indian subcontinent since the Phanerozoic. The clockwise rotations are represented in Table 3 by positive angles and anticlockwise rotations by negative angles, measured from 360" azimuth in the case of normal and 180" azimuth in the case of rocks of reversed magnetization. Table 3 shows that the Indian landmass was rotating anticlockwise in a more or less secular manner. The angles of rotation are less than 90" and the polarity of magnetization can be decided unambiguously by the interpolation of successive results. The mean directions for Speckled Sandstones (Sr. No. 17) and the Talchir Series (Sr. No. 18), however, show high angles of declination of 92" and 66" respectively and positive dips. The ambiguity regarding polarity of magnetization can be resolved on the basis of palaeogeographic and palaeoclimatological evidence. The Talchir Series are characterized by glacial tillites and boulder beds form the base of the Gondwana System in India. Table 3 gives the palaeomagnetic parameters such as mean direction of magnetization, VGP positions, palaeolatitude and palaeorotation etc. for all the formations studied so far, for the Indian subcontinent since the Phanerozoic. The clockwise rotations are represented in Table 3 by positive angles and anticlockwise rotations by negative angles, measured from 360" azimuth in the case of normal and 180" azimuth in the case of rocks of reversed magnetization. Table 3 shows that the Indian landmass was rotating anticlockwise in a more or less secular manner. The angles of rotation are less than 90" and the polarity of magnetization can be decided unambiguously by the interpolation of successive results. The mean directions for Speckled Sandstones (Sr. No. 17) and the Talchir Series (Sr. No. 18), however, show high angles of declination of 92" and 66" respectively and positive dips. The ambiguity regarding polarity of magnetization can be resolved on the basis of palaeogeographic and palaeoclimatological evidence. The Talchir Series are characterized by glacial tillites and boulder beds form the base of the Gondwana System in India. The Quebrada Marquesa Formation rests conformably on the Arqueros Formation and has been divided into four members. The lower three members contain a high proportion of tuff-breccias and tuffs of andesitic composition. Most of these volcanic products have under- gone extensive high-temperature oxidation and the rocks exhibit colour tones in reds and purples. The third member in addition contains red coloured sandstones and conglomerates. The uppermost member consists dominantly of grey coloured basalt or andesite flows in which original phenocrystic olivine now pseudomorphed by earthy haematite gives the rocks a distinctive speckled appearance. The lowest member of the Quebrada Marquesa Formation contains a few tens of metres of shallow marine limestones and calcareous sandstones bearing a number of pelecypod forms which suggest a late Neocomian age for the formation. Sedimentary units higher in the formation contain plant remains, exhibit dessication cracks and rain-drop imprints and are therefore continental and are entirely lacking in fossils of stratigraphic value. The lower three members contain a high proportion of tuff-breccias and tuffs of andesitic composition. Most of these volcanic products have under- gone extensive high-temperature oxidation and the rocks exhibit colour tones in reds and purples. The dates imply Late Precambrian and Early Cambrian ages, according to the time-scale of Van Eysinga (1975). Thermal demagnetizations were accomplished with either a Schonstedt Thermal Demagnetizer or by a non-magnetic furnace placed within the field-free space provided by a Helmholtz coil and Schonstedt HCM-3 Triaxial Coil Control Magnetometer feedback system capable of maintaining a field of 5 -10 nT or less. For alternating field (AF) de- magnetizations up to 100 mT (1000 Oe) a Schonstedt GSD-1 AC Demagnetizer was used. Demagnetization data were plotted using Zijderveld (1 967) diagrams and the components of magnetization were resolved by vector subtraction. This secondary component of the gabbro appears again as the characteristic (although somewhat scattered) directions of the granite de Porz-Scarff. there are petrologic and palaeomagnetic considerations that indicate the magnetizations to be primary. These are, in arbitrary order: (1) Magnetite is the prevailing magnetic mineral in most rock types studied and appears to be primary in thin sections; (2) the microgranite dykes remagnetized only those parts of the spilites into which they intruded, indicating that the magnetization of the spilites is older than that of the dykes; (3) rocks of approximately the same age give similar directions; (4) despite the similarity of the directions of the diorite de St Quay to Permo- Carboniferous directions elsewhere in Europe, the observed polarity of the diorite is opposite the prevailing Permo-Carboniferous polarity during the Kiaman interval; (5) the presence of lower-temperature directions, assumed to be secondary and correlating with characteristic directions of other younger rock units, suggests a primary origin for their higher-temperature directions insofar as they are also carried by magnetite. The Cambrian sediments at Cartaret provide an excellent section of palaeomagnetic analysis. The red beds at Dennemount Quarry from which most of the samples were collected contain hyolithids and sponge spicules suggestive of a Cambrian age (DorC 1963). The immediately overlying limestones which have a more complete fauna containing archaeocyathids and trilobites define the age of these beds as Lower Cambrian. The presence of dessication cracks and phosphate nodules in these beds suggests that they were probably deposited at fairly low latitudes. The beds at the second locality, Pointe-de-Rozel are also definitely of Cambrian age. The Pointe-de-Rozel strata are stratigraphically slightly higher than the Dennemount quarry section. The difference in strike and dip of the two regions provides a possible fold test of remanence age. Explanations for the directional smearing are to be sought in either partial remagnetization, or rapid polar shift during sediment deposition. For the former explanation to be valid we accept that some of the initial remanence has been masked by a secondary component that was probably chemically imprinted on the sediment at some instantaneous later date. On this model, the total remanence acquisition of a red bed is considered to be a long term process (Roy & Park 1974). That is not to say, however, that it is also a time averaging process. Critical to this point is the rate of secondary (colloidal) haematite deposition, and especially the rate at which individual grains grow through the critical remanence blocking threshold. Haematite may be depositing over a long period, but the grains only record stable remanence after passing the critical blocking size and this may take place over a very short time period. BOX 8757, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada Received 1979 October 10; in original form 1979 July 19 Summary. Results are reported from a short stratigraphic sequence of Lower Cambrian red sediments outcropping in Dennemount Quarry, Cartaret and Pointe-de-Rozel, Normandy. After af cleaning the data show a smear from steep to shallow positive magnetic inclination. Changes in inclination appear to be related to stratigraphic position - steep inclinations are stratigraphically lower than shallow inclinations. Further thermal and chemical treatment reveal that this smear does not record polar wander, rather it is the result of the interaction of two distinct remanence phases. Fold tests, chemical cleaning and opaque petrology indicate that the sequence of remanence acquisition was first the shallow south-westerly magnetization, followed later by the steep magnetization. Pole FB (13" S, 301" E, ag5 = 8") appears to date the initial depositional event. It may either be a chemical, or a detrital magnetization, or some combination of the two. Pole FA (22' N, 354' E, ag5 = 11") is related to the red pigmentation of the sediments. Although no strict age constraints can be applied to this remanence, a basal Ordovician age is preferred. Since microplate rotations may have been quite significant within the central European block (Badham & Halls 1975; Lorenz 1976), these are exactly the type of pole differences that we are hoping to detect. With respect to the European region it is the Ordovician pole path relative to southern Britain that is by far the best defined. The Cambrian pole path relative to Britain is as yet uncertain, the only published poles from Cambrian sediments being considered questionable. Their proximity to the representative Carboniferous pole could be considered as indicating that the Cambrian sediments are carrying Carboniferous magnetizations. Up till recently Lower Palaeozoic data for central Europe were even more scarce - the only data available being that published by Bucha (1961,1965) from the Ukrainian massif. A number of studies of this area have now been completed (Jones et aZ. 1979; Hagstrum et al. 1978) and it is to be expected that our understanding of the motions of the continental fragments trapped between the jaws of Laurentia and Gondwana will soon be improved. This study provides additional data points for the clarification of these motions. Introduction Although, faunal provincialism in the Ordovician had been known for some time, it was J. T. Wilson in 1966 who first interpreted the juxtaposition of distinct faunal realms as indicating that previous cycles of continental drift had been operative. Further detailing of faunal provinces by Whittington & Hughes (1972) and later by Burrett (1973) showed that the present European region contains a number of faunal provinces which at different times during the Ordovician were either isolated, or interacting with their immediate neighbours. umber of faunal provinces which at different times during the Ordovician were either isolated, or interacting with their immediate neighbours. For example, southern Britain during the Arenig to Llanvirn shows close affinities with southern Europe, while during the Tremadoc and after the Llanvirn it is more closely aligned with northern Europe. From the faunal evidence alone it is uncertain if these changes represent the movement of central Britain to and fro across a mid-European ocean or whether they record changes in climate, or ocean current, patterns. Resolution of this dichotomy is possible through a comparison of contemporaneous palaeomagnetic results from the different faunal provinces as they evolved through the Ordovician. 19 578 W. A. A number of studies of this area have now been completed (Jones et aZ. 1979; Hagstrum et al. 1978) and it is to be expected that our understanding of the motions of the continental fragments trapped between the jaws of Laurentia and Gondwana will soon be improved. No strict timetable can be erected to describe the temporal sequence of these events. Rather each deposit has its own unique character. Results are reported from a short stratigraphic sequence of Lower Cambrian red sediments outcropping in Dennemount Quarry, Cartaret and Pointe-de-Rozel, Normandy. Introduction Although, faunal provincialism in the Ordovician had been known for some time, it was J. T. Wilson in 1966 who first interpreted the juxtaposition of distinct faunal realms as indicating that previous cycles of continental drift had been operative. Further detailing of faunal provinces by Whittington & Hughes (1972) and later by Burrett (1973) showed that the present European region contains a number of faunal provinces which at different times during the Ordovician were either isolated, or interacting with their immediate neighbours. For example, southern Britain during the Arenig t

umber of faunal provinces which at different times during the Ordovician were either isolated, or interacting with their immediate neighbours. For example, southern Britain during the Arenig to Llanvirn shows close affinities with southern Europe, while during the Tremadoc and after the Llanvirn it is more closely aligned with northern Europe. From the faunal evidence alone it is uncertain if these changes represent the movement of central Britain to and fro across a mid-European ocean or whether they record changes in climate, or ocean current, patterns. Resolution of this dichotomy is possible through a comparison of contemporaneous palaeomagnetic results from the different faunal provinces as they evolved through the Ordovician. 19 578 W. A. M0rn.s Presently available palaeomagnetic data permit the description of a general distribution of the major landmasses for certain intervals of the Lower Palaeozoic. However, the data base is presently insufficient to detect detailed motions between smaller continental frag- ments. Since microplate rotations may have been quite significant within the central European block (Badham & Halls 1975; Lorenz 1976), these are exactly the type of pole differences that we are hoping to detect. A number of studies of this area have now been completed (Jones et aZ. 1979; Hagstrum et al. 1978) and it is to be expected that our understanding of the motions of the continental fragments trapped between the jaws of Laurentia and Gondwana will soon be improved. This study provides additional data points for the clarification of these motions. Red beds often have complex magnetic histories, and can in idealized circumstances record a number of remanence directions corresponding to a pole path segment (Roy & Park 1974; Roy & Robertson 1978). The differing remanence directions may record the gradual transition of the red bed from a newly deposited sediment, through diagenesis, and finally to later metamorphism. No strict timetable can be erected to describe the temporal sequence of these events. Rather each deposit has its own unique character. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carried out on nine lava flows around the Dhar region, which constitute the northern part of the Deccan traps. The stability of remanent magnetism of these specimens was analysed by an alternating magnetic field, thermal demagnetization and memory tests. Six flows exhibited characteristic components of magnetization, with a mean direction of D = 143", I= t46" (K= 107.1, ag5 = 5.5"). This gives a VGP located at 29" N, 67" W (6, = 4.5", 6, = 7.0"). The lower site with normal magnetization and the upper five sites with reverse magnetization indicate a geomagnetic field reversal during the initial phases of Deccan volcanism in the Early Tertiary period. A rapid northward migration of about 18" in latitude and a simultaneous anticlockwise rotation of 37" is calculated for the subcontinent. In a recent review of palaeomagnetic data of the Indo-Pakistani fragment of Gondwanaland, Klootwijk (1979) argued that during the Deccan volcanism the subcontinent had not moved more than 5" in latitude. Conclusions The Dhar traps are uniform in their magnetic character with magnetite as the main carrier of remanence in them. They are the earlier phases of eruption of the Deccan traps with a lower normal and upper reverse magnetization representing an Early Tertiary geomagnetic field reversal. The VGPs obtained from several investigations on the Deccan traps migrate from 25"N to 55"N which is interpreted as a drift of the subcontinent of about 18" in latitude. In spite of thorough palaeomagnetic studies of the Deccan traps, basic questions like the rapid northward migration of India and several reversals of the magnetic field remained unsolved as a result of diverging views expressed by several workers. From Table 1 it is evident that the five radiometrically dated dykes (whole rock K- Ar data), carrying stable, coinciding palaeomagnetic directions of inferred Late Triassic/ Middle Jurassic age, have K-Ar ages ranging between 164-274Myr. During this time span, however, several reversals of the geomagnetic field occurred in addition to a significant apparent polar wandering. As the dykes in question do not show any reliable indications of the presence of multi-component magnetizations, they are concluded to carry a primary magnetization representing a unique direction of the palaeomagnetic field. In addition, five of the supposed older reversely magnetized dykes (Permian), having major directional over- prints probably induced during reheating associated with the intrusion of the Triassic/ Jurassic dykes, reveal K-Ar ages ranging between 214-254Myr. Palaeomagnetic investigation of 18 coast-parallel, alkaline dykes from the Sunnhordland region, western Norway, reveal the presence of multi- component magnetization in half of the dykes. Received 1981 February 6; in original from 1980 August 19 Summary. Opaque mineralogical studies of late Mesozoic dolerite dykes of Wedel-Jarlsberg Land, South Spitsbergen, show that the dykes have under- gone a mild hydrothermal alteration. The alteration probably took place at the time of consolidation of the dykes, but may also have occurred as a side effect of Tertiary orogeny, which affected the western parts of Spitsbergen. Seven of these dykes were sampled during two summer seasons, when samples were collected from different exposures. A conventional procedure based on the minimum scatter principle and study of Zijderveld diagrams applied to 282 specimens demagnetized by alternating fields and thermally reveals several 'characteristic remanence' directions. In three dykes the directions are consistently reversed, but one carries both normal and reversed remanence. The reversed directions can be attributed to a geomagnetic field reversal in the late Mesozoic and K-Ar dating of one of the reversed dykes gives an age of 110 -+ 5 Myr BP in agreement with the known age of early Cretaceous field reversal. These rocks were magnetized during slow uplift following the ca. 1800 Ma Laxfordian tectonic/ magmatic episode. The Southern Zone experienced diachronous uplift and there is a transition from predominantly positive NW remanence directions in the north to shallow negative NW directions in the south. Each palaeo- magnetic site typically comprises six or seven independently oriented cores distributed over several metres of outcrop. Each palaeo- magnetic site typically comprises six or seven independently oriented cores distributed over several metres of outcrop. riod of protracted, and probably episodic, uplift and cooling from crustal depths equivalent to formation pressures of 15 kbar (30-40 km) in Badcallian times (OHara 1977) to cover thicknesses of 10-15 km by Laxfordian times, and with tempera- tures declining significantly only towards the end of the Laxfordian tectonism (Dickinson & Watson 1976; Watson 1977). This cover had been completely removed by the time of depo- sition of the Stoer Group (Torridonian) sediments at ca. 1000 Ma (Moorbath 1969; Watson 1975). The two previous studies of the Lewisian Complex were confined to the Central Zone. Beckmann (1976) isolated a highly stable remanence by af demagnetization from nine dykes near Lochinver and a Scourian granulite; only samples from the Central Zone in the Lochinver/Assynt area possessed a high coercivity remanence and no meaningful remanence directions were recognized in bordering parts of the Northern Zone. Morgan (1976b) inter- preted the Central Zone magnetizations in the context of slow cooling following the Laxfordian episode at ca. 1800 Ma. Schmidt CSIRO Division ofMineral Physics, PO Box 136, North Ryde, NSW 2113, Australia Received 1981 November 23;in original form 1981 September 11 Summary. A method that enables the objective resolution of almost parallel multi-component magnetizations is described and demonstrated. A feature distinguishing this method from others is its simultaneous analysis of demagnetization data from a group of specimens, rather than the analysis of data from one specimen at a time. The only prerequisite is that the specimens are derived from a homogeneous source. Thus for a formation carrying a simple single component magnetization, all specimens from the formation may be simultaneously reduced. For a more complicated two component magnetization it is shown that only specimens from a particular site can be considered homogeneous, and for a complex three component system each sample often requires undivided attention. Thus the workload is propor- tionally increased to achieve analyses of comparable reliability from data of variable quality. New pole positions from Mesozoic intrusions of the Sydney Basin, NSW are: from the Marsden Park Breccia pipe 48"S, 127"E (A9,=6"); the St Marys Breccia pipe 46"S, 150"E (A9, = 8"); the Prospect Dolerite 60"S, 142"E (A9, = 13") and 53"S, 180"E (A95 = 6"); and from the Dundas Breccia pipe 58"S, 162"E (A95 = 36") and 31"S, 195"E (Ag5 = 16").

The present investigation is concerned with the resolution and dating of magnetic overprints, and the dating of the times of formation of various intrusives within the Sydney Basin. Perhaps the most familiar techniques presently used to examine complex magnetizations are orthogonal graphs (Zijderveld 1967), vector subtraction (Roy & Park 1974), circles of remagnetization (Khramov 1958; Halls 1976, 1978; McFadden 1977), difference vector circles (Hoffman & Day 1978), and more recently principal component analysis (PCA) as presented by Kirschvink (1980). The use of earlier methods, such as the stable end-point and the optimum demagnetization step, has diminished, since they are inadequate for defining the directions of magnetizations which are removed during ‘cleaning’ of a multi- component remanence. Nevertheless there is still scope for improved data analysis. The method described below, although developed for a specific reason, can be adapted to cover a wide range of circumstances. The linearity of a segment may be defined in a variety of ways. The simplest method is to use the ratio of the distance between the bounding data points, to the sum of the distances between the intervening points. Although quick in terms of computation time, the linearity defined in this way will fail if data density is high enough such that the difference between the intervening points approaches the noise level of the system (i.e. measurement plus demagnetization noise). The linearity of a segment may be defined in a variety of ways. The simplest method is to use the ratio of the distance between the bounding data points, to the sum of the distances between the intervening points. Although quick in terms of computation time, the linearity defined in this way will fail if data density is high enough such that the difference between the intervening points approaches the noise level of the system (i.e. measurement plus demagnetization noise). Although these instances are not common, it is possible to use an alternative definition of linearity if the need arises. What appears to be basically a single component of magnetization is shown in the third study to be two, almost parallel but undoubtedly different, components of magnetization. In order to obtain a Lower Palaeozoic pole for the Armorican Massif and to test the origin of the Ibero-Armorican arc, the Ordovician dolerites of the Crozon peninsula have been palaeomagnetically studied. The samples show a multicomponent magnetization which has been revealed by AF and thermal demagnetization and thoroughly investigated with rock magnetic experiments, polished section examinations and K/Ar dating. Four groups of directions have been recognized, often superimposed on each other in an individual sample. One component (D) has always the lowest blocking temperatures and coercivities and is considered to be of viscous origin, acquired recently in situ or in the laboratory during storage. Two components (A and B) are interpreted to be of secondary origin and to correspond to the observed K/Ar age distribution between 300 and 190Myr. econdary origin and to correspond to the observed K/Ar age distribution between 300 and 190Myr. These ages repre- sent the time interval between two regional thermo-tectonic events, asso- ciated with the Hercynian orogeny and the intrusion of dykes related to the early opening of the Central Atlantic Ocean and the Bay of Biscay. A fourth component (C) could be of Ordovician or younger Palaeozoic age; it is not clear whether the age of the magnetization is pre- or post-folding, but a pre- folding age would yield a direction of magnetization similar to Ordovician results from the Iberian peninsula. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: ril 20; in original form 1982 February 8 Summary. In order to obtain a Lower Palaeozoic pole for the Armorican Massif and to test the origin of the Ibero-Armorican arc, the Ordovician dolerites of the Crozon peninsula have been palaeomagnetically studied. The samples show a multicomponent magnetization which has been revealed by AF and thermal demagnetization and thoroughly investigated with rock magnetic experiments, polished section examinations and K/Ar dating. Four groups of directions have been recognized, often superimposed on each other in an individual sample. One component (D) has always the lowest blocking temperatures and coercivities and is considered to be of viscous origin, acquired recently in situ or in the laboratory during storage. Two components (A and B) are interpreted to be of secondary origin and to correspond to the observed K/Ar age distribution between 300 and 190Myr. These ages repre- sent the time interval between two regional thermo-tectonic events, asso- ciated with the Hercynian orogeny and the intrusion of dykes related to the early opening of the Central Atlantic Ocean and the Bay of Biscay. A fourth component (C) could be of Ordovician or younger Palaeozoic age; it is not clear whether the age of the magnetization is pre- or post-folding, but a pre- folding age would yield a direction of magnetization similar to Ordovician results from the Iberian peninsula.
